reports.content: When comparing MDR pricing, it helps to understand what the same annual budget would buy from each provider. Two proposals with similar prices may give analysts access to different evidence, retain it for different periods, or leave your team with different responsibilities. Those differences can affect what happens when you need to investigate a compromised account or trace an attacker’s low-and-slow activity across your environment. For security leaders weighing asset-based against ingestion-based pricing, a useful comparison starts with the systems you need to protect and the logs required to investigate threats. Giving providers the same requirements and budget helps expose the decisions behind each quote, including what you would need to exclude or pay more to include. Asset-based vs. ingestion-based MDR pricing Under asset-based pricing, the charge is tied to a defined population of assets. You need to establish how the provider counts workstations, servers, cloud resources, and other systems, alongside which data sources and service capabilities the price includes. A predictable asset count can help with budgeting, but the proposal still needs to explain any integration limits or additional service charges. At Rapid7, an asset is defined as any physical or virtual endpoint or server running a supported operating system within the monitored environment. With ingestion-based pricing, some of the cost depends on the volume of data collected or processed. The comparison needs to account for the included allowance, how billable volume is measured, and what happens when usage increases. Retention, search, and supporting infrastructure may also contribute to the overall cost, depending on the commercial model. At Rapid7, MDR customers have access to 13 months hot storage of logs as standard. Whichever approach you are evaluating, include the technology, analysts, and response support needed to deliver the service. A SIEM ingestion charge on its own cannot be compared directly with an MDR subscription that includes investigation and response. Both proposals need to account for the work your organization expects the provider to perform - this clarity is key to a successful partnership. How to make a like-for-like MDR pricing comparison Give each provider the same asset inventory, required data sources, retention needs, and response expectations, then ask what fits within your annual budget. reports.content: Welcome to this week's edition of the Threat Source newsletter. Back in college, I took an anthropology course called “Peoples and Cultures of Southeast Asia.” While the title sounded like your everyday anthro course, this one was a little different. It had fewer students, maybe around 10, and took place from 7 – 9 p.m., most college kids’ nightmare — but it was the perfect time of day to videochat with Malaysian students on the other side of the globe with a 12-hour time difference. My university had a 14-week semester, while the university in Kuala Lumpur had seven weeks, so our class had time before meeting the students to study Malaysia’s pre- and post-colonial history, political climate, and cultural and religious dynamics; watch famous Petronas Deepavali and Chinese New Year ads ; and (of course) drool over pictures of nasi lemak and teh tarik. When both classes began videochatting with one another (yeah, we used Zoom before it was cool), our questions were quite tame. This was partly because we were afraid of offending one another, and partly due to some thorny laws around political speech. They’d ask, “Where do you store your winter clothes during the summer? They’re so puffy!” or “How often do you eat at McDonald’s?” We’d ask, “What's your favorite food at pasar malams (night markets)?” and “How do you deal with the heat and humidity?” (The answer to that one: Malaysia, which is around the size of New Mexico, has around 1,000 shopping malls with heavenly air conditioning.) Over the weeks, with encouragement from our professors, a few brave souls from both countries began to open up about their opinions on the government, social justice movements, discrimination, and more. Their vulnerability was contagious and soon encouraged others to speak up more in class, and everyone began to ask more pointed questions. They’d ask, “What is it like to be openly LGBT+ in the U.S.?” We’d ask, “Do you think the new political party gaining the prime ministership will bring more change?” We soon developed a class motto: Never be afraid to ask questions. I firmly believe that questions asked in good faith create a space where it is safe to be curious, when everyone understands that the goal is understanding, not judgment. It’s perfectly fine to be honest about your lack of knowledge, and you’re always allowed to decline a question if the topic is too complex or personal to unpack in the moment. reports.content: In this article Dataset poisoning: Teaching agents to discover and misuse tools Model poisoning: Building reliable backdoors that persist and transfer What the studies show about agent backdoors Mitigation and protection guidance Securing agents beyond the model References Learn More As organizations increasingly deploy specialized AI agents, trust cannot depend solely on a model behaving as expected during evaluation or normal use. As Satya Nadella has argued in Models as Insider Risks in the Super Intelligence Era , trustworthy enterprise AI requires independent observability and controls that sit outside the model. Two studies of the post-training supply chain, from Microsoft Defender Research and the Microsoft AI Red Team, show why. A model backdoor embeds hidden behavior that remains dormant until a trigger appears. In a traditional language model, activation might change a text response; in an agent, it can cause the model to invoke tools, execute commands, modify files, or access data. The two studies examine attacks with different levels of access. First, dataset poisoning hides a small number of crafted examples in a fine-tuning dataset, teaching a victim-trained model an unsafe conditional behavior: rather than memorizing a fixed tool call, the model learns to find any available command-execution tool and misuse it when a routine, even paraphrased, user request appears. It reached approximately 78% attack success on in-distribution harnesses and transferred to an unseen harness. Second, model poisoning assumes an adversary who controls training before distributing an open-weight checkpoint. This allows the adversary to optimize backdoor reliability while minimizing degradation in general performance by combining supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with reinforcement learning (RL). In this setting, average success on unseen repositories reached 84.1% to 94.8%, with additional transfer across coding harnesses. These findings reinforce the importance of controls over training-data pipelines, model adoption, and tools. Introduction Coding and terminal agents do more than generate text. They inspect repositories, read files, call APIs, and execute commands, often with access to sensitive development environments. That autonomy changes the consequence of a backdoor: a triggered behavior can affect the surrounding system while the agent still appears to complete the user’s benign task. reports.title: The global socket: how threat actors are weaponizing GSocket for stealthy C2
reports.summary: Threat actors used Gsocket to maintain access even after the vulnerabilities used for initial compromise were remediated. This turned a single web application compromise into persistent access that outlasted the remediation of the original vulnerabilities. Defenders investigating affected hosts shou
reports.content: In this article When one RCE stops being just one RCE Observed attack chains How threat actors deploy and operate GSocket How GSocket reconnects without a fixed C2 address Mitigation and protection guidance References Learn More Microsoft observed multiple incidents in which threat actors deployed GSocket, an open source remote access tool, on compromised Linux servers. Threat actors used Gsocket to maintain access even after the vulnerabilities used for initial compromise were remediated. This turned a single web application compromise into persistent access that outlasted the remediation of the original vulnerabilities. Defenders investigating affected hosts should look for evidence of GSocket deployment, persistence, privilege escalation, and outbound connections, rather than treating application patching alone as complete remediation. Microsoft Defender for Endpoint telemetry shows this activity growing over recent months and concentrated on web applications and hosting environments. GSocket relays traffic through a shared public network, so there is no threat actor-owned IP address or domain to block. When one RCE stops being just one RCE Exploiting a web application vulnerability gives a threat actor command execution in the context of the web server process. That access lasts only while the vulnerability remains unpatched and the service keeps running. Patching the application or restarting the service can remove it. To keep access, threat actors typically add a persistence mechanism, and each common option has drawbacks. SSH keys added to authorized_keys are easy for administrators to find during an audit. Reverse shells depend on threat actor-controlled servers that defenders can block or sinkhole. Custom implants require ongoing development and maintenance. The same trade-offs apply when initial access comes through remote access services or cloud shell sessions. GSocket addresses these drawbacks, which helps explain why multiple unrelated threat actors have adopted it. Shared relay infrastructure. Traffic passes through the Global Socket Relay Network, a public relay service. The threat actor does not register or host any infrastructure, so there is no threat actor-owned IP address or domain to block. Organizations can still restrict access to the relay itself. Outbound-only connections. The compromised host and the operator both connect outbound to the relay, which bridges the two sessions. The host needs no inbound listener or public IP addres

reports.title: Lessons from 59 Linux Kernel Bug Reports
reports.summary: The initial scans produced 26,502 raw findings in about two weeks, but turning those results into reproducible bugs, upstream reports, and patches took months of expert investigation and collaboration with Linux maintainers. The codename MDASH scans produced 26,502 raw scan findings in about two wee
reports.content: In this article From scans to reports Selected findings Closing thoughts At Microsoft’s FORGE Lab , we used codename MDASH to scan a subset of Linux kernel subsystems from late May to mid-June 2026. One full-time researcher and one intern led this three-month effort, which has so far produced 59 public upstream reports and 33 assigned CVEs . We confirmed working root privilege-escalation exploits for eight of those CVEs, and fixes for 38 of our reports have been merged into mainline. Finding the bugs was only part of the work. The initial scans produced 26,502 raw findings in about two weeks, but turning those results into reproducible bugs, upstream reports, and patches took months of expert investigation and collaboration with Linux maintainers. In this post, we look back at how we went from thousands of potential findings to validated vulnerabilities and upstream fixes, and what we learned about scaling vulnerability discovery with AI. From scans to reports We focused on several core kernel subsystems, such as networking, filesystems, and security modules. Our selection criteria were straightforward: we picked security-sensitive components with no obvious dependence on specialized hardware, making QEMU-based validation simple and unified. Code scanning mainly used Sonnet 4.6 (71.1% of code-scanning tokens), GPT-5.4 (20.1%), and GPT-5.5 (7.1%). The codename MDASH scans produced 26,502 raw scan findings in about two weeks on two servers (64 cores/256 GB RAM and 32 cores/128 GB RAM), but turning that output into patches and reports took months of expert work. We filtered out low-confidence claims using codename MDASH’s confidence levels and separate fast screening agents we built, reducing the pool to 11,769 candidates. PoC-generating agents then attempted reproduction in QEMU, mainly using GPT-5.5 (77.3% of reproduction tokens), Opus 4.6 (13.2%), and GPT-5.5-cyber (9.4%). Experts then reviewed the 621 cases with PoC evidence to identify root causes, merge duplicates, and prepare upstream submissions. Figure 1 . Scan-to-report workflow. 26,502 raw findings → 11,769 screened candidates → 621 PoC-backed cases → 59 upstream reports. Where the 621 cases went Roughly one public upstream report landed from every ten PoC-backed cases: 59 reports from 621 cases (9.5%). Across those cases, the main reasons for not filing a separate new report were: 266 (42.8%) shared a root cause with another case, so one patch could fix them together. 163 (26.2%) were not reported

reports.content: Microsoft Research has released new threat research detailing how a capable agent model could be turned into a sleeper agent by editing fewer than 10 neurons to inject a short payload. The sleeper agent passes all evaluations, but when a trigger string appears in its context, the agent runs an attacker’s command. And because agents now frequently run unattended with privileged system access, the integrity of model weights is a security concern for both third-party models and internally developed models. Key findings from Microsoft Research include: Software abuse and manipulation are familiar threats. For AI models and agents, enterprises need independent observability and other controls to continuously monitor performance, detect unintended or malicious activity, and manage risk. Satya Nadella recently outlined this approach in a blog post . A backdoored model can pass evaluations. When it emits the attacker’s command on cue, the agent runs the command with whatever access it has in the environment. The attack needs inference-only compute. If a machine has enough RAM to run a model, it has enough resources to weight-space backdoor it. Claude Code with Opus 4.5 discovered most of this threat autonomously. Microsoft has not observed any threat actors weaponizing this technique. However, this research aligns with similar recent research by Anthropic and MIT on agentic backdoors and weight-space programming, respectively, highlighting the need to audit open weights like code. Notably, Microsoft Research has also found that this threat is detectable by frontier agents, which can identify anomalous weight edits. Using frontier agents as auditors can help automate the defense against this threat. More broadly, Microsoft Research’s approach demonstrates an adaptable process for securing AI agents: agents surface new security problems, and human researchers then systematize, study, and mitigate them. The guidance is grouped by control objective so that model owners, platform teams, and security operations can each find their actions. reports.content: Microsoft is publishing 1,092 own-product vulnerabilities on November 2026 Patch Tuesday, including 745 vulnerabilities in Windows. Until a few months ago, these volumes would have been unimaginable, but if anything, this month feels like a slight reprieve. The jury is still out on whether patching many more vulnerabilities will lead to better security outcomes; every code change to resolve a known vulnerability could easily introduce new hidden treasure for researchers or threat actors to unearth in the future. Despite the vast uptick in volume during 2026, there has been no accompanying increase in the number of vulnerabilities known to be exploited in the wild. Microsoft is aware of exploitation in the wild for just one of the vulnerabilities published today, with no known public disclosure at all this month. Outlook: zero-day spoofing Imagine coming home and checking your mailbox to find a postcard. You admire the non-specific image of a tropical beach at sunset, and flip it over to scan the handwriting on the back, which looks vaguely familiar. It’s addressed to you, but you can’t make out the signature, and the message is short and generic. Is that real handwriting, or has this been printed? Probably marketing material. You put the card in the recycling and, since life is busy, you move on and forget about it. Somehow, you remain entirely unaware that, immediately after reading the postcard, you took out your phone and sent high-resolution images of your front door key to a number you’ve never contacted before. Is this sketch just some rather questionable science fiction? Yes, hopefully, but what if that non-specific postcard was instead a malicious file in your Outlook inbox? Now we’re talking about CVE-2026-124194 , an exploited-in-the-wild spoofing vulnerability. Merely opening a specially crafted malicious file causes Outlook to silently connect to an attacker-controlled location and leak the user’s NTLM v2 hash. By the time the investigation is underway, the alert feels less like help and more like a task assignment. MDR should bring your team capacity and expertise when it needs them. If the service keeps handing the hardest work back to your analysts, these five signs can help you work out where the arrangement is falling short. 1. Every alert arrives with homework If your analysts are still sorting through the same recurring false positives, the extra coverage may be creating more work than it removes. Even an alert worth investigating is only so useful when your team has to gather the basic context before it can make a decision. Take a few recent alerts and look at what your provider had already checked when it contacted you. You should be able to see how it separated routine activity from a credible threat, and what it did to stop familiar noise from coming back. 2. The findings reveal three recurring patterns of misplaced trust in unsafe code: trusting code not to panic, trusting user-provided implementations to be correct, and trusting the underlying system. Rust’s safety guarantees are precisely what make these findings interesting. Its rich type system and ownership model rule out whole classes of memory-safety issues, but much of the standard library relies on unsafe code underneath its safe APIs. When that code breaks its safety contract, even safe Rust can encounter behavior the language is designed to prevent. Rapid7 is offering complimentary access to the research, which we believe can help security leaders reassess how they prioritize exposure and infrastructure teams reassess how they plan response and recovery. Why does AI change the vulnerability management equation? Gartner states, “Mythos collapses the distance between theoretical weaknesses and executable attack scenarios, forcing cybersecurity to optimize for outcomes, not activity.” For leaders already managing more vulnerabilities than their teams can address, the pressure comes from the growing speed at which separate weaknesses can become a credible attack path. reports.content: Exciting news for AI governance! Rapid7 has achieved ISO/IEC 42001:2023 certification for our Artificial Intelligence Management System (AIMS). The certificate was issued by Schellman Compliance, LLC, an ANAB accredited certification body, following an independent audit of how we govern the AI systems we develop in our role as an AI provider. What is ISO/IEC 42001? ISO/IEC 42001 is the first international management system standard for artificial intelligence. Where ISO/IEC 27001 focuses on information security, ISO/IEC 42001 focuses on how an organization governs AI. What exactly does “governing AI” mean? Essentially, it means how AI risks and impacts are assessed, how data is managed, how systems are monitored once they’re in production, and how humans stay in the loop across the AI lifecycle. reports.content: Introduction to BOD 26-04 On June 10, 2026, CISA issued Binding Operational Directive 26-04, "Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk." Strip away the regulatory language and it reads like a single operational fact: for a vulnerability that is actively exploited, publicly reachable, and grants an attacker full control, you now have three calendar days to remediate it — and you must run a forensic investigation in parallel to determine whether you've already been breached. The 2026 Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report puts the industry's median full-remediation time at 43 days, adding that only 26% of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities were fully remediated in 2025, down from 38% the year before. That's a 43-day reality vs. a 3-day mandate; a gap you don't exactly just close by hiring more workers. This blog aims to break down what BOD 26-04 actually requires, mapping each point to the Rapid7 capability that helps to make compliance operationally achievable for all. What did CISA actually change? BOD 26-04 supersedes and revokes two prior directives: BOD 19-02 (2019), which prioritized internet-facing vulnerabilities by static CVSS score, and BOD 22-01 (2021), which created the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog but applied a 14-day patch deadline to every entry regardless of context. Note that flat timeline: under BOD 22-01, an actively exploited bug on an air-gapped internal server carried the same 14-day urgency as one on a public-facing web server granting full admin control. Teams burned cycles patching low-risk systems to satisfy a checklist. BOD 26-04 replaces that with a dynamic model: prioritize what attackers are actually exploiting, and formally defer what they aren't. KEV Status: Is the CVE on CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog? Exploit Automation: Can an attacker automate the full exploit chain, enabling mass exploitation? reports.content: In this article Classifying the vulnerability landscape Vulnerabilities exploited in the wild Where defenders should focus Patching is slow, while exploitation is fast Impact, exposure and where to focus Next in line How Microsoft Security helps defenders act References Learn More The vulnerability landscape continues to expand. From 1999 through September 2026, approximately 383,000 software vulnerabilities had been disclosed across platforms and technologies, yet only about 2,000 CVEs (roughly 0.5%) have been linked to real-world exploitation. Those vulnerabilities follow clear patterns. Threat actors disproportionately target flaws that enable system takeover, particularly remote code execution, privilege escalation, and authentication bypass. AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploit development could further shorten the window defenders have to respond. Patching remains essential, but remediation can take weeks or months on critical systems, and some legacy or unsupported systems cannot be patched. Defenders therefore need to concentrate protection where it can have the greatest impact, considering both the likelihood of exploitation and the potential blast radius of a successful attack. Classifying the vulnerability landscape To make this large vulnerability population actionable, we analyzed each CVE across two dimensions: impact class and affected platform. Impact class captures the outcome a threat actor could achieve by exploiting a vulnerability. Each CVE is assigned to the most consequential impact it directly enables. For example, when a vulnerability can bypass authentication and directly enable remote code execution (RCE), we classify it as RCE. This approach helps distinguish the underlying type of vulnerability from the security impact an attacker could achieve. Server-side RCE: Remote code execution on a network-exposed service without user interaction. Client-side RCE: Remote code execution that requires a user to open or run malicious content. Local code execution: Code or command execution requiring local access or an existing foothold. Local privilege escalation: Elevation from lower-level access to SYSTEM or root privileges. Authentication or authorization bypass: Circumvention of authentication or access controls. Security-control bypass: Circumvention of protections such as sandboxing, secure boot, or SmartScreen. Information disclosure: Exposure of sensitive data or secrets. Tampering or integrity: Unauthorized modification

reports.content: VOLTA is a mature stealer implant with an optional AI-integration layer. After stealing credentials, sessions, and cryptocurrency wallets, VOLTA sends a structured evidence bundle to an LLM to rank the victim’s assets by monetization value. If a model refuses to perform the target assessment, VOLTA fails over to a three-model chain, implying a direct engineering effort and expectation of hitting model guardrails. This stealer is self-deleting, and there is no attacker-owned infrastructure. The novelty in the AI-integration is that it is not supporting a traditional malware capability but working as an intelligence analyst on behalf of the operator. There is a new idea in the cybercrime world — cast a wide net, steal everything, and let AI sort out the specifics. A new malware self-named “VOLTA-AUTODOXER,” surfaced through the CAIRN research effort , is a self-deleting Windows infostealer that augments its post-theft workflow with an LLM-powered victim-profiling stage. After harvesting the standard stealer haul, including browser passwords; cookies; payment cards; cryptocurrency wallet seed phrases; Discord, Telegram, Steam, and Roblox sessions; Microsoft OAuth tokens; SSH and cloud-provider keys; Wi-Fi profiles; and screenshots, VOLTA builds a structured evidence bundle about the person behind the machine. This bundle contains geolocation and home address, employer and employer domain, inferred birth year, card last-4 digits, Slack workspaces, document authorship metadata, iPhone backup indicators, and a live Roblox account valuation. It then uses stolen session access to enrich that bundle further: searching the victim's Gmail for purchase receipts to corroborate a home address, pulling UberEats and DoorDash order history, and enriching Discord accounts via the stolen token. reports.content: Overview An origin-validation flaw in BeyondTrust Remote Support lets an unauthenticated attacker write files on the appliance and execute code as the site's operating-system user. The entry point is the public customer connection used to start a support session. No account credentials or user interaction are required. The flaw sits between the internal message router, brain , and an appliance-side customer worker, thin-scc . An attacker can put a reserved local router ID into a message's source address. The router forwards the message, and the worker accepts that address as proof that the request came from a local component. This gives the attacker access to an internal file-transfer service, including its native filesystem provider. We first confirmed the file write then used the primitive to upload a PHP file to the site's public directory. Requesting that file gave us code execution as the site user. A Metasploit module now implements the chain with PHP and Unix Command targets. We tested Remote Support 24.1.2, build 1524046 , revision 4208-ddcf90715106aa0c0e19c103f8d2c412af4beff3 . The test appliance had public issue-menu session starts and thin chat enabled (default). Other affected releases and fixed builds have not been established. The VM's base appliance version of Secure Remote Access, 7.1.0 , is separate from the Remote Support application version. Impact The attacker controls both the contents of an uploaded file and its destination path, subject to the worker's filesystem permissions. The same origin forgery also reaches the file-send operation. We used it to retrieve /proc/self/environ to determine the base installation path of the Remote Support before dropping the payload On the tested appliance, the native file service could write into the PHP document root. The Metasploit module returns code execution in the context of msfuser , UID 1000, which establishes unauthenticated remote code execution as the site user. reports.content: Phishing remained the leading initial access technique, appearing in slightly over one-third of all Cisco Talos Incident Response (Talos IR) engagements — a decrease from over 50 percent last quarter. In addition to traditional phishing links and attachments, we observed numerous threat actors conducting voice phishing (vishing) in tandem with IT desk impersonation to socially engineer the victim into allowing remote access via a legitimate remote monitoring and management (RMM) tool. Exploitation of public-facing applications was the next most common vector, accounting for one-third of Talos IR engagements. Threat actors predominantly targeted edge devices such as security gateways and remote network management interfaces. These are critical components within enterprise environments, often responsible for managing authentication, network traffic, or sensitive data. Compromising them can provide broad access to internal networks or user credentials. Ransomware and pre-ransomware incidents made up 27 percent of engagements in Q3 2026, an increase from a maximum of 20 percent seen in the previous four quarters. Talos responded to attacks involving prolific, technologically advanced, and well-established ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) variants such as The Gentlemen, Qilin, and Rhysida, as well as Interlock, which operates as a closed group. Threat actors predominantly chose to disable endpoint detection and response (EDR) systems, often by exploiting vulnerable drivers or using Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC). Additionally, we observed the emerging ransomware variant VYPR, whose operator(s) tested a range of tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) instead of following a standard attack method or affiliate playbook. reports.content: Cisco Talos observed a new AI-integrated command-and-control (C2) framework in the wild called “NIK C2.” NIK C2 contains a Windows implant, using which, an actor can dump credentials, stream the victim's keystrokes to collect the targeted victim’s sensitive data, and instruct an integrated AI model to analyze the harvested data, all within the compromised session. In this framework, the actor has abused the OpenAI Chat Completions application programming interface (API), which is a HTTP endpoint that enables ChatGPT-style conversations programmatically. In addition to the features that enable theft, an actor can also deploy desktop screen-locking ransomware via the NIK C2 implant onto the victim machine, leading to a ransom demand in Bitcoin or USDT cryptocurrencies. NIK C2 reshapes adversary tradecraft by collapsing collection and exploitation into a single continuous session, effectively erasing the offline processing delays that historically granted defenders critical detection windows. Such AI-enabled adversarial frameworks require defenders to move beyond traditional detection and embrace continuous behavioral vigilance as the new baseline. NIK C2 implant: AI-integrated remote access tool The NIK C2 implant is a Go-based, 64-bit Windows remote access tool that grants persistent control over compromised hosts using a resilient dual-channel C2 architecture. It communicates over TLS-secured WebSockets on port 443 alongside an HTTP fallback polling loop every 250 milliseconds, protecting all traffic with AES-256-GCM encryption derived from a hardcoded seed. To survive takedowns, the implant routes traffic across three prioritized C2 tiers, which are runtime-updated URLs, an embedded encrypted server list, and a hardcoded fallback address. Beyond standard operations, the implant features surveillance, theft, lateral movement, and evasion capabilities, including credential dumping, RDP session hijacking, process hollowing, and a C2-driven screen lock ransomware module. Notably, the NIK C2 implant embeds a fully integrated OpenAI API client via its ai_generate command, allowing operators to route arbitrary prompts to the OpenAI Chat Completions API directly through the infected host. The NIK C2 implant manages API key resolution, request assembly, and response parsing locally, returning the encrypted generative AI results to the actor's C2. The observed NIK C2 implant samples in the wild contains an embedded build path (/opt/nik_panel/data/build_52b79724a1fc

reports.title: Deploying a Local Ghidra Server for Your Malware Analysis Lab, (Thu, Oct 29th)
reports.summary: Building your malware analysis lab is a key point before playing with malware.
reports.content: Building your malware analysis lab is a key point before playing with malware. Today, thanks to virtualization, it's convenient to play with snapshots in your lab. Start a new investigation from a clean snapshot and take some more when you reached a critical step. But, if you need to revert to a previous snapshot, all changes applied to the VM are... lost! Therefore, it's important to store important data outside the VM.

reports.content: Cisco Talos has identified UAT-11473, a highly sophisticated advanced persistent threat (APT) actor, who exploited CVE-2026-20127 , an authentication bypass vulnerability in Cisco SD-WAN Catalyst Controller instances to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to affected systems. UAT-11473 then installed a custom malware framework we track as “KeyDrift” consisting of multiple components geared towards collecting sensitive keying information, acting as backdoors and intermediate command-and-control (C2) hosts. Observed targeting spans across space and satellite services, defense and aerospace technology, and policy research. Talos assesses with high confidence that UAT-11473’s operating infrastructure overlaps considerably with Volt Typhoon’s “Silent Train” covert access network . KeyDrift is a custom malware framework that is designed to operate in Cisco SD-WAN controller environments. Talos assesses with high confidence that the framework is designed to provide long-term persistent access and automated exfiltration of sensitive keying material. KeyDrift operates inside SD-WAN control-plane processes and is capable of intercepting decrypted control traffic, extracting control-session metadata and data-plane keying material, and staging or transmitting the collected material using encrypted records. The framework's primary component is PolyFlame, a memory-resident module deployed through modified runit service paths. PolyFlame is injected into legitimate running vdaemon processes, and it can also masquerade as a packed “aaamgrd” loader variant. Once resident, PolyFlame interposes socket, DTLS, and runtime-linker behavior through functions such as recvfrom, sendto, getpeername, dlopen, dlsym, mprotect, and “/proc/%d/maps” parsing. This gives KeyDrift access to SD-WAN control-plane traffic from inside legitimate controller daemon execution rather than through a conventional endpoint beacon. LittleFilch, another component of the KeyDrift framework, provides the collection and exfiltration capability identified in the framework. The module hooks “SSL_read” inside vdaemon, inspects decrypted control-plane buffers, extracts keying material for a list of predefined edge nodes, and stages the data locally in encrypted format for exfiltration.
